item.title: JD Vance faces tough questions on Iran war, immigration and gas prices in town hall
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In an hour-long town hall hosted by CBS News, Vice President JD Vance argued the Trump administration's handling of the economy and Iran strategy will pay dividends in the future. He was also pressed on the Trump administration's controversial immigration tactics, widespread discontent about the cost of living and his own political future during "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance," which aired Saturday evening and was hosted by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil. Vance took questions from voters in Michigan, a swing state that helped propel Vance and President Trump to victory in 2024 — and is the host of a tight Senate race that could help determine which party wins control of the upper chamber in next month's midterm elections. Vance says he hasn't decided if he'll run for president If he decides to run for president in 2028, the vice president is widely viewed as an early frontrunner in the Republican primaries and a possible heir to Mr. Trump's political movement. Mr. Trump has called Vance his "most likely" GOP successor and has joked about a potential contest between Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Vice President JD Vance said there’s “of course” a chance he won’t run for president in 2028, pointing to his four young children and his wife’s feelings about politics. Vance said he plans to make a decision after the midterm elections. pic.twitter.com/O9bho2LPl0 — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 18, 2026 Asked by Dokoupil if there's any chance he won't run, Vance said: "Of course there's a chance." "The way that I think about life, big life decisions — my wife will tell you this — is I'm a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it," said Vance, adding that he'll "have to think about it." He also noted that he and his wife, Usha Vance, have four young children, and the second lady "has never loved politics," though "she loves public service." On economy, Vance says "we're turning the ship around" but it will take time Several town hall attendees asked Vance about cost-of-living issues. The topic weighs heavily in the midterms, and has demonstrated it's a liability for Republicans based on CBS News polling. Voter dissatisfaction with inflation and the state of the economy under the Biden administration helped bring Mr. Trump and Vance to power, but polls indicate that most voters are still unhappy with the economy and hold the Trump administration responsible. Sandy Johnson said her small business is "barely making ends meet.” She asked Vice President JD Vance when she can expect changes in the economy, "so that the normal American has money to spend on small businesses." “I'll be the first person to tell you that, just as this… pic.twitter.com/ED5yypKiOJ — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 18, 2026 Sandy Johnson said the family entertainment center she owns is "barely making ends meet," and asked when she can expect changes "so that the normal American has money to spend on small businesses." The vice president argued it could take some time. "What broke the United States, as much as I might like to criticize Joe Biden, but it was a bipartisan, multi-generational failure to under-invest in American workers, to under-invest in American manufacturing, to ship all of our good jobs overseas," Vance said. "If all the good jobs are overseas, then people here in Michigan can't spend money at your family business." He pointed to promises of new foreign investment in the United States, and growth plans by the three major Detroit-area automakers, General Motors, Ford and Chrysler parent Stellantis. "We are turning the tide on this," Vance said, referring to the decline in U.S. manufacturing. "And I think there are all these things I pointed to that show signs of progress. But Sandy, I'll be the first person to tell you that, just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around." Since Mr. Trump returned to office last year, the unemployment rate has remained low, but inflation has remained stubbornly higher than the Federal Reserve's 2%-per-year target, eating into Americans' wages. The number of manufacturing jobs has also remained roughly flat. Asked by Dokoupil about Mr. Trump's assessment of an "A+" economy , Vance said the president was referring to new investments, "but he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first before you can employ the workers working in those factories." Vance later said: "I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around." Iran and energy: "I recognize that gas prices are too high right now" One of the biggest pressure points on Americans' wallets is the Iran war , which has kept oil prices high even as the U.S. and Iran have refrained from active fighting in recent weeks. One of the biggest pressure points on Americans' wallets is the Iran war, which has kept oil prices high even as the U.S. and Iran have refrained from active fighting in recent weeks. Vice President JD Vance told one Michigan voter that he believes, “when this conflict is over,… pic.twitter.com/bUFe8tSdyG — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 18, 2026 Keshon Wheatley, a barber from Detroit, told Vance that he voted for Mr. Trump in 2020 and 2024, in large part because he gave the president credit for low gas prices during his first term. Now, gas prices are far higher — and he said he plans to vote for Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , not Republican Mike Rogers. Vance pointed to Iran's attacks on oil tankers. "We've never had a situation like this, where you have effectively the largest state sponsor of terrorism that's trying to completely choke off world energy supply," the vice president said, arguing that "if we just … left, and we let the Iranians control shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, what that would mean is you would pay a lot more for gasoline." Asked how long it will take for prices to ease, Vance said, "When this conflict is over, we are going to see gas prices come down." He said oil is still being exported from the Middle East because of efforts by the U.S. military to allow ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. On the competitive Michigan Senate race, he argued El-Sayed — a frequent critic of the Iran war — has not offered a solution to the problem, and gave Rogers credit for calling for the war to end. "He's been remarkably independent about this," Vance said of Rogers. Dokoupil asked Vance why the U.S. hasn't decisively won the Iran war, which has dragged on for longer than Mr. Trump initially expected. Vance argued that "in some ways we have won decisively," but "the enemy gets a vote here." The vice president — who participated in negotiations with Iran over the summer — defended the president's Iran strategy, and said the Trump administration is looking for a "final firm commitment from the Iranians that they're not going to rebuild their nuclear program." Man whose wife died in Iranian strike decries "fundamental failures" The Iran war has also imposed human costs, with 21 U.S. service members killed and hundreds injured since the conflict began in late February. The Iran war has also imposed human costs, with 21 U.S. service members killed and hundreds injured since the conflict began in late February. In the war’s early hours, six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed in an Iranian strike on a site in Kuwait, including Master Sgt.… pic.twitter.com/8P89COcKv0 — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 18, 2026 In the war's early hours, six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed in an Iranian strike on a site in Kuwait, including Master Sgt. Nicole Amor . Her husband, Joey Amor, asked Vance about reports that the facility in Kuwait was not adequately secured. "Though the Iranian drone was the weapon that killed my wife, there were a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures that led up to that," Amor said, asking Vance "how this administration is gonna start holding those leaders accountable." Vance said he didn't doubt there were failures , but "sometimes information doesn't filter up to me." He vowed to "take every single failure extremely seriously." He also noted that cheap drones have changed warfare, and "we have changed a lot of our tactics to try to suppress that drone fire, to try to protect our troops to make it so that more people don't have to pay the ultimate sacrifice." Vance also said: "I know that there are some issues with, for example … where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake and that we could do better on. And we have changed that." Nun presses Vance on immigration tactics Sister Nancy Sylvester, a member of the Sister Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, asked Vance about the Trump administration's approach to immigration enforcement . Sister Nancy Sylvester, a member of the Sisters, Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, said nuns have seen families in Michigan and along the southern border affected by ICE enforcement. She asked Vice President JD Vance about the Trump administration’s approach to… pic.twitter.com/ZhlA1MDivV — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 18, 2026 She asked Vance, a fellow Catholic, "how you would justify [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactics] to people of faith," and "what policies would you advocate to try to promote more compassionate and [respectful] behavior toward our immigrant sisters and brothers." Vance responded, "We're trying to strike a balance between: How do we do law enforcement, but how do we also do it humanely, and how do we not do so little law enforcement that you actually empower some of the worst people in the world." Vance later said most ICE agents are "amazing people who are patriots," but some of them "make mistakes" or "really screw up." He added that "obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up." Asked if any major mistakes by ICE come to mind, Vance responded that "there are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE." Another town hall attendee pressed Vance on some of the administration's rhetoric around immigration, including Vance's own comments that likened some holders of employment-based H-1B visas to "foreign indentured servants." Vance responded, "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me." He said his comments were "not a criticism of the H-1B holder." "That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker, bring somebody else in, and knows that person, if they complain, if they get too uppity at work, if they have a disagreement with their boss, they couldn't just lose their job, … they can be shipped back to their country of origin," Vance said. "And I think that gives employers way too much power." He said, "My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant." But he said he is seeking "to make it so that we can have a country with some baseline of social cohesion and sense of community, because what happens when too many people come to the United States, even if they're very good people, … [is] it changes the country in very profound ways." "D.C. is a corrupt town," but Vance says no evidence Trump is participating in it Dokoupil asked Vance about polling that indicates many voters are concerned about corruption and believe Mr. Trump is prioritizing his own personal business interests while in office. When asked by Tony Dokoupil about recent polling that indicates many voters are concerned about corruption and believe President Trump is prioritizing his own personal business interests while in office, Vice President JD Vance said, "I've never seen anything like that from the… pic.twitter.com/ha6hZ6WDfh — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 18, 2026 Vance said , "I've never seen anything like that from the president." "Yes, D.C. is a corrupt town," Vance said, but "I have not seen a single shred of evidence that he participates or sanctions in that corruption." Dokoupil also asked about a string of recent reports, including Mr. Trump's cryptocurrency earnings and U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's ouster over allegations that she asked a person seeking help from the Trump administration to wire her $100,000. Guilfoyle has denied all wrongdoing. Mr. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest. Vance responded : "If somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences." The vice president also said he will "follow the law" if a Democratic Congress launches investigations and subpoenas the Trump administration. Data centers need to be "good community citizens" A major point of tension in many communities across the country is the explosion in data center development , as the artificial intelligence boom leads to insatiable demand for computing power. Mr. Trump has enthusiastically backed the AI industry, casting it as an engine of economic growth and a key area of competition with China. He has also argued data center construction can be beneficial to local communities, bringing jobs and investments in crucial technology. But many voters have raised concerns about noise, disruption and pressure on the electrical grid, leading to calls for development to slow down. A major point of tension in many communities across the country is the explosion in data center development, as the artificial intelligence boom leads to insatiable demand for computing power. The vice president said “data centers can be good” and can also “cause real problems.”… pic.twitter.com/B207ixVf0h — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 18, 2026 Vance took a question from one Michigan resident who lives across the street from a data center and said the constant buzzing has made "opening our windows to let in a breeze … a luxury that we could no longer enjoy." The vice president said "data centers can be good" and can also "cause real problems." He said his view is that data centers should be "good community citizens," offering more tax revenue to local governments. The data centers should also not lead to higher residential utility bills, Vance said. "Some of the economic benefits they're generating, they can't just go to a few tech billionaires," he said. "It has to go to the community writ large." Watch the full episode of "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" streaming on Paramount+ , YouTube, CBS News 24/7 and CBSNews.com. item.title: Trump's most controversial moves have something in common: This DOJ office
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When White House officials wanted to know if President Donald Trump could send the U.S. military to help capture President Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a special unit in the Justice Department assured them it was legal. When the administration was preparing to strike suspected drug traffickers’ boats on the open sea without congressional approval, the same small unit declared the action permissible. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. When the White House asked if the Presidential Records Act was constitutional, the office ruled it was not, giving Trump the apparent green light to save fewer records from his second term. As the Trump administration pushes the bounds of executive power, the Justice Department unit known as the Office of Legal Counsel, or OLC, has affirmed some of its most high-profile and controversial actions - even as many experts question their legitimacy and some are later struck down by the courts. Tucked away on the Justice Department’s fifth floor, the two dozen or so lawyers at the OLC are charged with assessing the legality of actions the executive branch wants to take, especially those that are novel or likely to be contentious. Much of its work, particularly on national security matters, remains shielded from public view, but some of the office’s conclusions have emerged in often dense legal opinions. The OLC during Trump’s second term is not the first to be accused of adopting shaky reasoning to justify a president’s policies. Under President Barack Obama, the OLC wrote a controversial rationale for launching a deadly drone attack on a U.S. citizen overseas. Under President George W. Bush, the office justified the used of “enhanced interrogation” - what some call torture - against enemy combatants, including waterboarding. But because Trump has advanced so many controversial policies - including imposing global tariffs, refusing to spend congressionally allocated funds and pushing to more broadly deploy the National Guard - the OLC now faces particular scrutiny. Critics contend that during Trump’s second term, the OLC is sometimes responding to legal questions that appear personal to Trump, rather than addressing live policy debates, as is typical. For instance, Trump had quibbled over the Presidential Records Act after he was indicted in Florida for allegedly mishandling classified materials. These critics said the OLC opinion on this act seemed aimed at Trump’s prior issues with the law, rather than any active policy issues. “It is not inconsistent with the type of advice OLC of any flavor, Democrats or Republicans, would give to other presidents,” said Carlos Uriarte, a Justice Department political appointee during the Biden administration who worked closely with the OLC. “What’s different is that this administration seems to be more willing to go into theoretical questions that are not before them.” Trump’s OLC is headed by T. Elliot Gaiser, a 37-year-old former solicitor general of Ohio described by current and former colleagues as a constitutional originalist who, like Trump, has an expansive view of executive power. Gaiser, who represented Trump’s losing presidential campaign in 2020 and refuses to acknowledge Joe Biden won that election, said his role in the Justice Department is to provide honest legal advice, not push for any particular outcome. “We’re the least interested in advocating, [and] the most interested in saying, ‘Here’s our frank view of where we think we stand in respect to the law,’” Gaiser told The Washington Post in a rare interview. His sparsely decorated office is filled with bound books of legal opinions, which surround a desk Gaiser proudly says is believed to have once been used by former Supreme Court justice Antonin Scalia, who headed the OLC under President Gerald Ford. People who know and have worked with Gaiser spoke positively about him, with former associates describing him as “brilliant.” Gaiser clerked on the Supreme Court for Samuel A. Alito Jr. when the justice wrote the landmark opinion restricting abortion access. As OLC head, Gaiser has written conservative opinions backing restrictions around abortion access, expanded gun access and greater White House authority. Gaiser said he has not hesitated to tell the White House when its ideas should not be enacted, though he declined to share specifics. Gaiser, and others familiar with the office, noted that the president is not required to listen to the OLC. Much of OLC advice is shared privately. As a result, public perceptions of the OLC are largely shaped by the opinions it releases, even as they represent only a portion of its work. The office’s role could become even more central if Democrats take control of Congress. The office recently approved an expanded view of executive privilege, for example, which Democrats fear will be used to shield Trump’s associates from testifying before Congress. Gaiser’s office could also get asked to provide legal advice if outcomes are challenged during and after next month’s midterms. The office has already determined that the executive branch can legally seek a state’s voter rolls and share them with immigration authorities - a key part of the Trump administration’s strategy to identify noncitizen voters as it tries to argue that voter fraud is rampant. Asked during the interview in his office who won the 2020 election, Gaiser demurred, citing his work as a lawyer for Trump’s campaign that year. He cannot say publicly who won, Gaiser said, because that would reveal too much about the privileged legal advice he gave Trump campaign officials when he was their attorney. “Joe Biden was sworn in as the president. He was certified the winner of the election by the Congress,” Gaiser said. “What I privately think happened in the 2020 election - what advice I provided to the president as the head of the campaign or to others in the campaign, the other campaign lawyers - that’s the kind of stuff I just really can’t get into .” Although many Trump appointees display sharp elbows and make frequent appearances on cable news shows, Gaiser takes a lower profile, even as his work is attracting increased attention, including from Democratic lawmakers and federal courts. After the OLC declared in April that the Presidential Records Act was unconstitutional, a federal court responded to lawsuits and said that, at least for now, the White House had to preserve records as normal. Advocacy groups are fighting to unseal the OLC’s memo justifying the deadly boat strikes in international waters. One former OLC attorney, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer a sensitive assessment, said the office’s opinions are based on shoddy legal arguments. Under previous administrations, “you have opinions that at least try to grapple with counterarguments,” but that is not the case today, the former OLC lawyer said. Gaiser sharply disputes the assertion that his office’s opinions are not high-quality, saying he and his lawyers deliver honest, accurate assessments. “There is a continuum with the advice you give. You can say, this is lawful but risky. This is lawfully safe. This is unlawful,” Gaiser said. “OLC has a measure of independent counsel that we offer.” During the first Trump administration, the OLC pushed back on some of the president’s most explosive actions. Steve Engel, then head of the OLC, testified about the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol that he had advised Trump appointees that some of their plans to question the results of the 2020 presidential election were not legal. Under Engel, the OLC also advised that an executive order ending birthright citizenship - the legal principal that virtually everyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen - would be unconstitutional, according to multiple people familiar with the matter, and the president did not issue one. But when Trump became president a second time, he issued an order to end birthright citizenship on his first day in office. The OLC did not review it or the other executive orders Trump issued immediately upon his return, according to two people familiar with the matter. The Supreme Court later affirmed birthright citizenship in a ruling that Trump called a “miscarriage of justice.” Gaiser, who was confirmed in July 2025, had not taken office at that point, and said his office has since reviewed all of the president’s executive orders before they are issued. The OLC attracted a burst of attention in August when it issued an opinion on executive privilege, which can shield communications between presidents and their aides. The office declared that the doctrine covers not only official advisers, but can also expand to cover outside associates consulted by the president in certain circumstances. The opinion was released as the American Bar Association was suing the Trump administration over its efforts to sanction law firms that hired Trump’s perceived foes or took on cases he disliked. The ABA is seeking testimony from Boris Epshteyn, one of Trump’s outside advisers. The ABA assailed the OLC opinion as self-serving and suspiciously timed. But Michael Edney, who worked at the OLC under Bush, said the opinion’s reading of executive privilege was not unreasonable, given the importance that some presidents place on outside consultation. “It’s not all that crazy to me,” he said. Most experts said that while OLC lawyers are not required to be blind to the president’s agenda, they cannot simply interpret the law to suit his priorities. Former OLC employees said the office should not be a rubber stamp, regardless of whether the president heeds its opinions. “In the executive branch, like everywhere else in the world, lawyers give advice and clients make decisions,” Edney said. “Their job is to provide legal advice.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/18/meet-small-doj-unit-approving-some-trumps-most-controversial-policies/
Matched: policy(+3), law(+3), court(+2), election(+2), who(+2)

item.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy [Reuters] A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys, while France decried the attack as "appalling". Both called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating. But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened, suggesting it was part of a "co-ordinated campaign to smear Israel". The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look". It was also condemned by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law". In Saturday's incident, the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah. They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest. Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown. The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle. Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice, as well as ensuring the safety of diplomats, journalists and Palestinians. "Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said. He also said Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for the violence. Palestinians have been harvesting olives in the West Bank this week before Israeli settlers attack [EPA] France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot echoed those sentiments, calling on Israeli authorities to "urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations". Poland's foreign affairs ministry also called for a "firm response" from Israeli authorities and for "an end to the spiral of violence in the West Bank". The EU condemned the attacks, urged Israel to abide by international and human rights law, and end the expansion of settlements. A spokesperson said that while they acknowledged some Israeli officials had condemned the attacks, they said they still expect "full accountability as well as effective measures" to stop the continued violence against Palestinians and journalists. Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved. But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security." The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters." "According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added. Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux, the left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries [Reuters] But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack. It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility". A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible." It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge". Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence. The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground. "It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged." "The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said. item.title: GOP lawmakers criticize Trump's decision to waive Russia sanctions: 'Unconscionable'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Several GOP lawmakers criticized President Trump’s move to exempt Russia from the sanctions bill he signed law last month, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.) calling the move "beyond irresponsible." Trump signed an executive order Friday evening to waive sanctions against Russia in a legislative package that was meant to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its military operations against Ukraine. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis wrote on the social platform X. The legislation, signed by Trump in September , would impose tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions. The sanctions bill was drafted by and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The late senator had announced a breakthrough on the legislation shortly before his death in July, saying lawmakers reached a deal with the White House to move it forward. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) posted the news on social media Saturday morning saying, “Lindsey would be appalled.” “The President is prolonging the war, not ending it,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on social media , referring to Friday’s executive order. In his Friday order , the president noted that the legislation allows him to “waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person.” “I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.” In a post on social platform X Saturday, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) showed support for the president’s decision, calling the sanctions legislation “short-sighted.” He noted in his post that he was among only seven Republicans who voted against the bill. “Glad to see Trump has used the executive authority granted to him by Congress to waive almost all of the provisions of this stupid law that pertain to Russia,” Massie wrote. One the other side of the aisle, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who played a major role in passing the sanctions bill, called the president’s move to waive sanctions for Russia, a “craven, cowardly action.” “These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal wrote in his post. Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) also slammed the president’s move on social platform X , saying it “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.” The move comes after the president struck a deal with Russia last week permitting the country to sell diesel products to the U.S. and in the world market amid global fuel shortages. The deal prompted backlash from lawmakers across the board. In an interview with Piers Morgan, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” by the president’s decision. Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), who was among five House Republicans who signed a letter to the president urging him to cancel the Russia diesel deal, posted to X Saturday asking the president to “reverse course” on the sanction waivers. “Time and again, we have seen how Putin responds to American concessions: with contempt for the United States and increased violence against innocent Ukrainians,” McCaul wrote. item.title: A new generation of synthetic drugs is changing America's overdose crisis
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raid Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says. The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars. "You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says. He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune. We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction. Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanyl [Darren Conway/BBC] Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets [Darren Conway/BBC] We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States. At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over. It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl. The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added. When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce." Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me. They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat. Recovery group offering hope At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma. They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty. One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life. As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid. "It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement. Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood Church [Darren Conway/BBC] One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time [Darren Conway/BBC] Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose". "In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers. Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so. "The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it." Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope Dealers [Darren Conway/BBC] Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds. His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina. That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine. "The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements." And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois. Watch the documentary on YouTube I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity. Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means. He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever. When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability." And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear. "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me. A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening. "In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel." The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures. Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens. It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters. "Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained. Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures. In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in letters [Darren Conway/BBC] In August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search. As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of. As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates. The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper. Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected. Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moisture [Darren Conway/BBC] Outside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them. In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell. Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs. She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing." Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants. The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous". "Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me. Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town [Darren Conway/BBC] Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics. "The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it." Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way." 'A lot of people are struggling' Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track. It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb. Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs [Darren Conway/BBC] As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed." A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail. When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours." She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs." Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics. Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them. item.title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as hundreds arrested in France protests
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets. In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse. Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. In the French capital, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC that they were "pacifists" who were "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving". However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République. Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups. Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons. In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building". Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze. Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse. La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fire [Getty Images] A young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened." Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15- to 18-year-olds. Their numbers have been bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups. These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes (or "yellow vest") movement, which demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for more than a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history. France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers. Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence. Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied. Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers. A car was set alight at the Place de la République in Paris [Reuters] While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty. French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party. The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson. Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris [Reuters] Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical". He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence." Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence. Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished." The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers during a television interview on 8 October. However, the protests have continued and intensified. Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on Saturday [Getty Images] Watch: 'Mood has really shifted' as Paris protesters clash with police Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
